claims.text: Bulk, near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can be produced by additive manufacturing followed by sintering.
A printed and sintered bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimen can contain approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen represents a realistic processing-induced defect concentration in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed model will explicitly represent oxygen interstitials, vacancies, and local lattice distortions instead of assuming a perfect lattice.
The model is intended to predict transport in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes for samples with and without approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Point defects and oxygen interstitials produce local lattice distortions and additional scattering centers in HfNbTaTiZr.
The defect-associated scattering centers modify both phonon and electron transport.
Accounting for realistic defect populations captures additional scattering mechanisms that reduce thermal and electrical conductivity, especially at low temperature.
Defect scattering modifies the temperature dependence of thermal and electrical conductivity.
Explicit microstructural defect modeling will improve agreement between calculations and measurements on processed HfNbTaTiZr.
Conventional analytical models assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Conventional defect-free analytical models tend to overestimate conductivity and neglect temperature-dependent defect scattering.
In the 0–200 K regime, the defect-inclusive prediction will be approximately 10–20% lower than predictions from defect-free analytical models.
For HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, predicted thermal conductivity in the 300–1200 K regime will agree with measurements in the range 12–17 W/(m·K).
The defect-inclusive model will provide markedly better quantitative agreement with experiment than conventional defect-free predictions.
The proposed applicability domain is bulk HfNbTaTiZr and similar refractory high-entropy alloys with oxygen contents up to approximately 1 wt.% and temperatures from 0 to 1200 K.
Extrapolation to higher oxygen contents or different processing routes requires additional validation.
The benchmark experiment compares defect-minimized and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen samples against both defect-free and defect-inclusive model predictions over the two temperature regimes.

The hypothesis is falsified if the defect-inclusive model fails to reproduce measured conductivity within ±10% in either temperature regime or if the predicted difference between defect-minimized and oxygen-containing samples is absent.
